cards.title: Tactical Patterns — The Implementation-Level Building Blocks
cards.teaser: Strategic DDD tells you where to draw lines; tactical DDD tells you what to put inside them. The tactical patterns are the implementation vocabulary Evans defines in Part II of the Blue Book — entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, services, repositories, and factories.

runs.text: Domain-Driven Design operates at two levels.
— bounded contexts, context maps, ubiquitous language — address the architecture of the entire system and how teams collaborate.
address the inside of a single bounded context: how domain concepts are represented in code.
Evans introduced the tactical patterns in
Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software
(2003), Part II — "The Building Blocks of a Model-Driven Design." The core catalog:

items.text: — an object with a unique identity that persists over time and through state changes.
— an immutable object defined entirely by its attributes; two value objects with identical attributes are identical.
— a cluster of entities and value objects with a single root that enforces invariants across the cluster.
— an immutable record of something significant that happened in the domain.
— stateless logic that belongs in the domain but does not naturally fit on any entity or value object.
— a collection-like interface for retrieving and storing aggregates, hiding persistence mechanics.
— an object or method that encapsulates complex creation logic.

runs.text: Together these patterns give a team a shared vocabulary for talking about their code at the domain level: "this is a value object, not an entity" carries precise meaning that "this is a class" does not.

Evans was careful to note that these patterns are not a methodology to follow mechanically. They are a vocabulary for capturing design decisions that emerge from deep collaboration with domain experts. The patterns serve the model; the model serves the business.
Tactical DDD patterns are the LEGO bricks you use inside a bounded context. Strategic DDD decided what box the bricks go in; tactical DDD decides which bricks to use and how to connect them.

cards.title: Entity Preview — Identity Over Time
cards.teaser: An entity is not defined by what it looks like at a moment in time — it is defined by who it is across all moments in time. A Customer with a changed address is still the same Customer. Identity, not attributes, is the defining characteristic.

runs.text: is an object that has a distinct, continuous identity. Two entities are not equal because they have the same data — they are equal (or not equal) because they have the same identity, typically expressed as a unique identifier such as a UUID or a database primary key.

. An account opened in 2010 with a $0 balance and an account opened in 2010 with a $0 balance are two different accounts, even though all their attributes match at creation. Their identity distinguishes them. As the account accumulates transactions, its balance changes, but it remains the same account.

items.text: Decide how identities are generated: system-assigned UUID, natural keys from the domain, or user-provided identifiers. Each choice has trade-offs.
Implement equality on the identifier alone, never on all attributes. If you compare by all attributes you have a value object, not an entity.
State changes through operations that express domain behavior —

runs.text: Chapter 5 goes deep on entity identity strategies, lifecycle management, and how to model identity for entities that cross context boundaries. This card is the preview.

An entity is like a person: they change over time — haircuts, addresses, jobs — but they stay the same person. Two people who look identical are still two different people. That's what identity means in DDD.

cards.title: Value Object Preview — Equality by Value
cards.teaser: A value object has no identity — it is entirely described by its attributes. Two Money objects both representing $5 USD are the same $5. You don't care which one you have; you care what it is. Immutability is the defining implementation rule.

runs.text: (VO) represents a descriptive aspect of the domain that has no conceptual identity. Two instances with identical attribute values are interchangeable. This is the fundamental difference from entities.
(latitude + longitude). None of these have a lifecycle or need to be tracked individually — they describe something.

items.text: Never modify a value object in place. Operations return new instances:
Override equals/hashCode based on all attributes. Two
Methods on value objects should compute and return results, never modify external state.
Value objects are typically stored inline with their owning entity (as embedded columns), not as rows with foreign keys.

runs.text: Value objects should be the default choice. If a concept does not need to be tracked individually across its lifetime, model it as a value object. Over-using entities is one of the most common modeling errors.

A value object is like a $5 bill: you don't care which specific $5 bill you get, only that it's $5. It's immutable — you can't change a $5 into $6 in place, you exchange it. Two $5 bills are equal by definition.

cards.title: Aggregate Preview — The Consistency Boundary
cards.teaser: An aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects treated as a unit for data changes. One entity is the root. All external access goes through the root. The invariants that must hold true are enforced within the aggregate boundary — nowhere else.

runs.text: answers the question: "when I make a change, what scope of objects must stay consistent together?" The answer defines the aggregate's boundary.
. The invariant "total must equal the sum of all line item amounts" must hold across all of them. They form a single aggregate rooted at
The aggregate design rules (Evans + Vaughn Vernon's refinements in

items.text: Only the aggregate root has a repository.
You retrieve an entire aggregate through its root. You never query for a child entity directly by navigating to it without the root.
External objects hold only the root's identity.
References from outside the aggregate boundary point to the root's ID, not to internal entities.
A single database transaction modifies at most one aggregate. Changes spanning aggregates use eventual consistency and domain events.
Small aggregates are almost always better.
Large aggregates cause lock contention and complexity. When in doubt, split. Chapter 7 covers aggregate sizing heuristics in depth.

runs.text: An aggregate is like a sealed box of related objects. You interact with the box through its handle (the root). The box enforces its own rules internally. You never reach past the handle to rearrange things inside.

cards.title: Domain Event Preview — A Fact That Occurred
cards.teaser: A domain event is an immutable record of something that happened in the domain — in the past tense, named after the business fact. OrderPlaced, PaymentProcessed, InventoryReserved. It happened; it cannot be undone; other parts of the system can react to it.

runs.text: is a record of something the domain experts care about that occurred. The naming convention is past tense and domain-first:
Domain events were not in Evans's original 2003 Blue Book — they were added to the DDD community lexicon primarily through Vernon's
(2013) and are now considered a first-class tactical pattern. They serve several purposes:

items.text: When an aggregate changes, it raises a domain event. Other aggregates react to the event rather than being invoked directly, enabling eventual consistency without tight coupling.
Domain events published to a message bus allow bounded contexts to communicate without sharing a domain model.
Events are facts in the past tense — they form a natural audit log. Event sourcing takes this further, making the event log the system of record.
Naming events in the ubiquitous language —
— makes business triggers visible in code in a way method calls do not.

runs.text: A domain event carries its own data — the state needed by consumers — and is immutable once created. Chapter 8 covers event design, publication, and handling in detail.

A domain event is a notification that says "this important business thing just happened." It is past tense, immutable, and names the fact in business language. Other parts of the system listen and react — they don't need to know who raised it.

cards.title: Repository Preview — Collection-Like Persistence Interface
cards.teaser: A repository pretends your aggregates live in memory. You ask it for an Order by ID; it returns one. You add a new Order; it appears on the next retrieval. The underlying SQL, ORM, or document store is invisible to the domain model.

runs.text: is an abstraction that provides collection-like access to aggregates without exposing persistence mechanics. The domain layer defines the repository interface; the infrastructure layer provides the implementation.
The mental model Evans invokes is an in-memory collection. If you had all your objects in RAM, you might write:
A repository interface looks exactly like that. Behind it, the implementation may execute SQL, call a REST API, or talk to a document store — the domain does not care.

items.text: Never a repository for a non-root entity — access child entities through the aggregate.
The repository contract is part of the domain model. The implementation is infrastructure.
Do not add CRUD methods that bypass domain logic.
A repository is not an DAO. It serves aggregates, not tables.

runs.text: A repository is a lie you tell the domain: "all your aggregates are just sitting in a collection in memory." The lie is useful because it keeps SQL and ORMs out of business logic. The infrastructure layer handles the reality.

cards.title: Domain Service Preview — Operations That Don't Belong on Entities
cards.teaser: Some domain operations involve multiple entities or aggregates and do not naturally live on any one of them. Forcing them onto an entity creates a blob; extracting them into a domain service keeps each object responsible for what it knows about itself.

runs.text: The rule of thumb in OO design is to put behavior on the objects that have the data. But some domain operations involve coordination across multiple objects. A
is the appropriate home for these operations.
Evans's test: if you cannot think of a natural home for a concept on an entity or value object, and the concept is meaningful to the domain experts, it is likely a domain service.

items.text: — debits one account and credits another. Neither account is the natural home; both are equally involved.
— needs the order, the shipping address, and the carrier rate table. No single entity owns all this.
— an operation with domain meaning (how we secure credentials) that does not belong as state on the

runs.text: . They operate on entities and value objects passed to them; they do not hold state between calls. This is what distinguishes them from application services (which orchestrate use cases and cross-cutting concerns) and entities (which hold state).

Domain services are easily overused. If every domain concept ends up as a service, you have an anemic domain model — entities that are just data bags and services that do all the work. The heuristic: push behavior onto entities and value objects first. Only extract a service when multiple entities are naturally involved.

A domain service handles operations that involve several entities and do not belong on any one of them. It is stateless — it takes objects in, does domain work, and returns a result. It does not hold data between calls.

cards.title: Factory — Encapsulating Complex Creation
cards.teaser: When constructing an aggregate or entity requires complex logic — enforcing invariants, choosing which subtype to create, wiring relationships — that logic deserves its own home. A factory extracts creation knowledge from the client and the created object alike.

runs.text: as a DDD tactical pattern to encapsulate creation logic that is too complex to live in constructors or caller code. Factories apply the Gang of Four Factory Method and Abstract Factory patterns to domain object creation — but the motivation is different: the goal is to protect domain invariants during creation, not to abstract over families of objects.

items.text: requires validating the customer's credit limit, applying a promotional code, and selecting the correct pricing tier — that logic does not belong in a constructor.
An aggregate must never be created in an inconsistent state. A factory ensures all invariants are satisfied before returning the object.
Reconstruction from persistence differs from creation.
Factories often appear in two forms: a creation factory (applies business rules) and a reconstitution factory (restores state from a database record without re-applying creation logic).
The type to create depends on input.
If the concrete subtype of an entity depends on domain data (e.g.,

runs.text: ), static factory methods on the aggregate root, or factory methods on a domain service. The form matters less than the intent: creation logic is visible, named, and separated from both the created object and the client.

A factory handles the complexity of bringing an object into the world correctly. If creation needs business rules, it should not live in a constructor (which should be simple) or in the caller (which should not know the rules). The factory knows the rules.

cards.title: Module — Organizing the Domain Namespace
cards.teaser: A module in DDD is not just a package or namespace for code organization — it is a deliberate grouping of related domain concepts that tells a story. Good module boundaries are visible in the ubiquitous language and should require no explanation to a domain expert.

runs.text: (known as "Package" in some implementations) is a way to organize high cohesion and low coupling within a bounded context. While a bounded context is the outer partition (strategic level), modules are the inner partitions (tactical level).
The naming rule is strict: modules must be named with domain language, not technical language.
are not — they organize by technical role, not by domain concept.

items.text: Objects in the same module collaborate closely and share domain language.
Minimize relationships between modules. Where they exist, express them through interfaces, not direct object references where possible.
The module name should be a noun or noun phrase from the ubiquitous language:
If the ubiquitous language shifts — if "fulfillment" becomes "dispatch" in the domain experts' vocabulary — rename the module. The package name is part of the model.

runs.text: Evans notes that modules are often created by refactoring rather than up-front design. As the model deepens, clusters of related concepts emerge naturally and deserve a named home. Package-by-feature is the modern restatement of this principle.

A DDD module is a domain-named grouping of closely related concepts. Think of it as a chapter heading in the domain's vocabulary. If a domain expert cannot guess what is inside by the module's name, the name is wrong.

cards.title: The Layered Architecture
cards.teaser: DDD prescribes a four-layer architecture so that domain logic lives in one place and knows nothing about infrastructure. The layers are: Presentation, Application, Domain, and Infrastructure — and dependencies flow strictly downward.

runs.text: Evans dedicates a full chapter to the layered architecture as the structural prerequisite for a clean domain model. Without clear layer boundaries, domain logic leaks into controllers, queries leak into entities, and the model becomes impossible to reason about independently.

items.text: — HTTP controllers, GraphQL resolvers, CLI handlers, message consumers. Transforms external input into application-layer calls. Transforms output into responses. No domain logic here.
— Use-case orchestration. Coordinates domain objects to fulfill a use case. Handles transactions, security checks, event publication, and cross-cutting concerns. Thin — delegates to the domain.
— The heart. Entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, domain services, repository interfaces, factories. This is the only layer that expresses business rules.

— Implementations of domain interfaces. Repository implementations (SQL, NoSQL), email senders, file systems, external API clients, message bus adapters. Knows about frameworks and third-party libraries; the domain does not.

The layered architecture is like an onion with the domain at the center: presentation talks to application, which talks to the domain, which has no idea infrastructure exists. Each layer only knows about the layers below it.

cards.title: The Dependency Rule — Domain Knows Nothing About Infrastructure
cards.teaser: The domain model must not import or reference infrastructure. If your entity imports a JPA annotation, a Hibernate session, a Spring bean, or an HTTP client, the domain layer has been contaminated. The dependency rule is non-negotiable in DDD.

runs.text: in DDD states that the domain layer must have no outward dependencies on the application, presentation, or infrastructure layers. It knows only itself: domain language, domain logic, domain interfaces.
This rule is enforced architecturally through the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP). When the domain needs to persist an aggregate, it defines a repository
in the domain layer. The infrastructure layer implements that interface. The domain never references the implementation — only the interface.

items.text: ). The entity now knows how it is stored. Changing the schema touches the domain object.
Domain objects become framework-coupled. Testing requires a Spring context.
SQL or ORM queries inside aggregate methods.
The entity fetches its own related data. Infrastructure leaks into the heart of the model.
The domain service now fails if an external API is unavailable, making it impossible to unit-test in isolation.

runs.text: The reward for keeping the domain clean is testability: every entity, value object, aggregate, and domain service can be tested with plain objects — no database, no framework, no network. Domain logic tests run in milliseconds.

Robert Martin's Clean Architecture (2017) and Alistair Cockburn's Hexagonal Architecture ("Ports and Adapters") both formalize the same core rule Evans stated: the domain/application core must not depend on delivery mechanisms or data stores. These architectures are complementary to DDD, not competing with it.

The dependency rule says the domain model is the boss — it defines interfaces, and infrastructure obeys them. If a domain object imports anything from a framework or database library, the rule is broken and the model is no longer independently testable.

cards.title: Tactical Patterns vs Strategic Patterns — When Each Applies
cards.teaser: Strategic and tactical DDD solve different problems at different scales. Strategic patterns draw boundaries between teams and contexts; tactical patterns design what lives inside one context. Applying tactical patterns without strategic boundaries is common — and commonly the root cause of the mess they were meant to solve.

runs.text: The two halves of DDD are complementary but not symmetric:

items.text: (bounded contexts, context maps, ubiquitous language, subdomains) answer: "How do we partition the overall system? How do teams collaborate? Where does each model apply?"
(entities, VOs, aggregates, events, services, repositories, factories) answer: "How do we implement the domain model inside one bounded context?"

runs.text: A common failure mode: applying tactical patterns across the whole codebase as if there were one universal domain model. Without bounded context thinking, an

entity accumulates attributes from billing, fulfillment, shipping, and marketing — it becomes a god object because all contexts share one model. Tactical patterns do not fix this; bounded contexts do.

Another common failure mode: investing in bounded contexts, context maps, and ubiquitous language but implementing each context as an anemic CRUD service. Strategic clarity is wasted without tactical discipline inside each context.

items.text: Define bounded contexts, name subdomains, map integration patterns. This sets the outer walls.
Within each context, apply the tactical building blocks — entities, aggregates, repositories, events — to express the domain model in code.
Core subdomains deserve rich tactical modeling. Generic and supporting subdomains may not need aggregate design at all — a simple CRUD service is often the right choice.

runs.text: Evans himself, in his 2014 keynote at DDD Europe, noted that teams often skip strategic DDD and jump straight to tactical patterns. The result is a well-structured model of the wrong thing — beautifully designed entities in a context with the wrong boundary.

Strategic DDD draws the map; tactical DDD builds the roads. You need the map first, or the roads go to the wrong places. And you need well-built roads inside each region, or the map is just a nice picture.

cards.title: How the Tactical Patterns Relate to Each Other
cards.teaser: The tactical patterns are not independent tools — they form a system. Entities and value objects compose into aggregates. Aggregates emit domain events. Repositories retrieve aggregates. Factories create them. Domain services coordinate them. Modules organize them. Layer architecture contains them.

runs.text: Understanding each tactical pattern individually is necessary but not sufficient. The power is in how they connect:

items.text: Entities + Value Objects compose into Aggregates.
An aggregate is made of one root entity and zero or more child entities and value objects. Value objects are the preferred building block; entities are used when identity is required.
When an aggregate changes state in a domain-significant way, it records a domain event. The application layer collects these events after the transaction and dispatches them.
The repository's unit of work is always a complete aggregate — not a fragment of it.
When construction is complex, a factory handles it and returns a fully-initialized aggregate in a valid state.
Domain Services coordinate when operations span Aggregates.
A domain service may load two aggregates from their repositories and orchestrate a domain operation that neither could perform alone.
Modules group related Aggregates, Services, and Value Objects.
The module is the naming and cohesion structure that makes the domain model navigable.

runs.text: The layered architecture contains all of this. Domain objects live in the domain layer. Repository interfaces live in the domain layer. Repository implementations live in the infrastructure layer. Application services in the application layer coordinate the flow.
The chapters that follow treat each pattern in depth — but read them knowing they are parts of a system, not independent choices.

Entities and value objects are the raw materials. Aggregates bundle them into safe units. Repositories fetch and store those units. Factories build them correctly. Domain events carry news when something changes. Domain services step in when no single unit can do the job alone. Modules label the neighborhoods. The layered architecture gives everyone their address.
